title: Galaxies spiralling around Leo
caption: Barred spiral galaxy NGC 3455, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 3455 · constellation Leo · about 65 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble image shows NGC 3455, a spiral galaxy about 65 million light-years away in Leo, the Lion. Its partner galaxy, NGC 3454, lies just outside the frame.

Astronomers sort galaxies by their structure and appearance using the Hubble Sequence, a scheme devised by Edwin Hubble. In that system NGC 3455 is a type SB galaxy, a barred spiral, meaning a bar of stars seems to slice through the central bulge. Around two thirds of spirals are barred. The SB class is then split according to how the arms look. SBa galaxies have tightly wound arms, SBc galaxies have loose ones, and SBb galaxies like NGC 3455 fall in between.
The pair belongs to the NGC 3370 group, itself one of the Leo II groups, a big scattering of galaxies lying some 30 million light-years off to the right of the Virgo cluster.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.29 x 2.39 arcminutes) and distance (65 million light years), the frame spans roughly 62,000 × 45,000 light-years. Its light set out about 65 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposure collects far more light than an eye could.
